claim: TRIM21 is a cytosolic antibody receptor that stimulates immune signalling.
source: Recent work from our lab has shown that, in addition to classical FcR immunity mediated at the cell-surface, antibodies exert potent immune function from inside cells via a unique cytosolic IgG receptor called TRIM21 (James, 2014; Mallery et al., 2010; McEwan et al., 2013).
evidence: Supported by citations to previous work from the authors' lab

claim: TRIM21 binds antibodies with significantly higher affinity than surface Fc receptors.
source: TRIM21 is structurally, functionally and evolutionarily distinct from surface FcRs and binds antibodies with a significantly higher affinity (James et al., 2007).
evidence: Supported by citation to James et al., 2007

claim: TRIM21 is constitutively and ubiquitously expressed in most cell types and tissues.
source: TRIM21 is also distinct in being constitutively and ubiquitously expressed in most cell types and tissues.
evidence: Statement about TRIM21 expression pattern based on established knowledge

claim: TRIM21 protects cells from pathogen infection through a dual effector and sensor response.
source: TRIM21 protects cells from pathogen infection by stimulating a dual effector and sensor response.
evidence: General statement about TRIM21 function supported by subsequent detailed description

claim: TRIM21 recruits cellular degradation machinery including VCP and the proteasome to destroy viral particles.
source: TRIM21 recruits cellular degradation machinery, including the AAA ATPase VCP and the proteasome, resulting in the destruction of viral particles and neutralization of infection.
evidence: Description of TRIM21 mechanism based on established knowledge

claim: TRIM21 activates immune transcription pathways including NF-κB, leading to upregulation of pro-inflammatory cytokines.
source: TRIM21 simultaneously activates immune transcription pathways, including NF-κB, leading to potent upregulation of pro-inflammatory cytokines including TNF, CXCL10, IL-6 and IFN (McEwan et al., 2013).
evidence: Supported by citation to McEwan et al., 2013

claim: TRIM21 activation results in cytokine upregulation in mice within hours of infection.
source: TRIM21 activation results in cytokine upregulation in mice within hours of infection and is a significant component of the inflammatory response induced by protective antibodies (Watkinson et al., 2015).
evidence: Supported by citation to Watkinson et al., 2015

claim: Deletion of TRIM21 compromises the efficiency of protective antibody immunity and causes virus-induced mortality.
source: Deletion of TRIM21 compromises the efficiency of protective antibody immunity and causes virus-induced mortality (Vaysburd et al., 2013).
evidence: Supported by citation to Vaysburd et al., 2013

claim: TRIM21 is dimeric and can bind both heavy chains of a single IgG simultaneously, forming a 1:1 complex.
source: Furthermore, as TRIM21 is dimeric, it is capable of binding both heavy chains of a single IgG simultaneously and forming a 1:1 complex.
evidence: Statement about TRIM21 structure and binding stoichiometry based on established knowledge

claim: TRIM21 lacks ITAM and ITIM motifs that drive the function of other Fc receptors.
source: Finally, TRIM21 lacks the ITAM and ITIM motifs that drives the function of other FcRs, and whose signalling can be precisely regulated by recruitment of Src family kinases and inositol-lipid phosphatases (Vogelpoel et al., 2015).
evidence: Comparison of TRIM21 to other FcRs with citation

claim: TRIM21 belongs to a family of ~100 proteins with a tripartite motif architecture comprising N-terminal RING, B-Box and coiled-coil domains.
source: TRIM21 is a member of a large family of ~100 proteins with a common 'tripartite motif' architecture, comprising N-terminal RING, B-Box and coiled-coil domains.
evidence: Description of TRIM protein family structure based on established knowledge

claim: TRIM21 stimulates immune signaling via the activity of its RING domain, which catalyses the synthesis of polyubiquitin chains.
source: Instead of recruiting Src and Syk kinases, TRIM21 stimulates immune signaling via the activity of its RING domain, which catalyses the synthesis of polyubiquitin chains.
evidence: Description of TRIM21 signaling mechanism based on established knowledge

claim: TRIM21 recruits the E2 Ube2W to modify itself with an N-terminal monoubiquitin.
source: TRIM21 first recruits the E2 Ube2W to modify itself with an N-terminal monoubiquitin (Fletcher and James, 2016).
evidence: Supported by citation to Fletcher and James, 2016

claim: The N-terminal monoubiquitin acts as a primer for the synthesis of an anchored K63-chain catalysed by Ube2N/2V2.
source: This acts as a primer for the synthesis of an anchored K63-chain catalysed by the heterodimer Ube2N/2V2.
evidence: Description of sequential ubiquitination mechanism based on established knowledge

claim: The proteasomal deubiquitinase Poh1 liberates K63 chains from TRIM21.
source: The 19S-resident proteasomal deubiquitinase Poh1 subsequently liberates K63 chains from TRIM21 (Fletcher and James, 2016), and these then activate signal transduction pathways via TBK1, TAB/TAK and NEMO.
evidence: Supported by citation to Fletcher and James, 2016

claim: Full-length TRIM5α causes dose-dependent activation of NFκB when overexpressed.
source: While transfection of full-length TRIM5α caused dose-dependent activation of NFκB, full-length TRIM21 failed to activate NFκB at any dose (Figure 1A).
evidence: Experimental data shown in Figure 1A

claim: Full-length TRIM21 fails to activate NFκB at any dose when overexpressed.
source: While transfection of full-length TRIM5α caused dose-dependent activation of NFκB, full-length TRIM21 failed to activate NFκB at any dose (Figure 1A).
evidence: Experimental data shown in Figure 1A

claim: Endogenous TRIM5α undergoes rapid recycling.
source: Consistent with the NFκB result, while endogenous TRIM5α underwent rapid recycling we found little evidence of TRIM21 turnover even after several hours (Figure 1B and Figure 1—figure supplement 1).
evidence: Experimental data shown in Figure 1B and Figure 1—figure supplement 1

claim: TRIM21 shows little evidence of turnover even after several hours.
source: Consistent with the NFκB result, while endogenous TRIM5α underwent rapid recycling we found little evidence of TRIM21 turnover even after several hours (Figure 1B and Figure 1—figure supplement 1).
evidence: Experimental data shown in Figure 1B and Figure 1—figure supplement 1

claim: The TRIM21 RING domain is more active than the TRIM5α RING domain in vitro, capable of forming ubiquitin chains within minutes.
source: However, comparing the ubiquitination activity of TRIM5α and TRIM21 isolated RING domains (T5-R or T21-R) in vitro revealed that TRIM21 was the more active E3, capable of forming ubiquitin chains within minutes (Figure 1C).
evidence: Experimental data shown in Figure 1C

claim: TRIM5α RING dimerization mutations disrupt RING dimerization and inhibit catalytic ability.
source: TRIM5α self-assembles and mutations that disrupt RING dimerization inhibit catalytic ability (Yudina et al., 2015).
evidence: Supported by citation to Yudina et al., 2015

claim: Wild-type TRIM21 RING is in monomer-dimer equilibrium.
source: SEC MALS and AUC demonstrated that while the wild-type RING is in monomer-dimer equilibrium, mutants M10E and M10E/M72E do not undergo detectable dimerization (Figure 1E and F).
evidence: Experimental data from SEC MALS and AUC shown in Figure 1E and F

claim: TRIM21 RING mutants M10E and M10E/M72E do not undergo detectable dimerization.
source: SEC MALS and AUC demonstrated that while the wild-type RING is in monomer-dimer equilibrium, mutants M10E and M10E/M72E do not undergo detectable dimerization (Figure 1E and F).
evidence: Experimental data from SEC MALS and AUC shown in Figure 1E and F

claim: TRIM21 RING mutants M10E and M10E/M72E remain active and can catalyse ubiquitin chain synthesis, albeit less efficiently than wild-type.
source: However, both mutants remained active and could catalyse unanchored K63 chain synthesis, Ube2W-primed anchored K63 chain extension and ubiquitin discharge (Figure 1G–I), albeit less efficiently than wild-type.
evidence: Experimental data shown in Figure 1G–I

claim: A pre-formed TRIM21 RING dimer is not a pre-requisite for ubiquitination activity.
source: These results demonstrate that a pre-formed TRIM21 RING dimer is not a pre-requisite for ubiquitination activity.
evidence: Conclusion drawn from experimental data showing monomeric mutants retain activity

claim: RING dimerization is not required for E2 enzyme binding.
source: RING dimerization is not required for E2 enzyme binding, as all interactions occur within a single monomer (Yudina et al., 2015).
evidence: Supported by citation to Yudina et al., 2015

claim: Dimerization of RING E3s is thought to be needed for additional contacts with the E2-charged ubiquitin.
source: Instead, dimerization of RING E3s is thought to be needed for additional contacts with the E2-charged ubiquitin.
evidence: General statement about RING E3 mechanism based on established knowledge

claim: Mutations in the partner RING at the ubiquitin-contacting interface reduce TRIM25 catalytic activity in vitro.
source: Mutations in the partner RING at this interface reduce TRIM25 catalytic activity in vitro (Figure 2A)(Sanchez et al., 2016).
evidence: Supported by citation to Sanchez et al., 2016 and reference to Figure 2A

claim: Equivalent mutations in TRIM21 had no impact on ubiquitination.
source: Equivalent mutations in TRIM21 had no impact on ubiquitination, confirming that RING dimerization is not an intrinsic requirement for TRIM21 activity (Figure 2B–D).
evidence: Experimental data shown in Figure 2B–D

claim: The mutation E10R reduces ubiquitination by TRIM25, possibly by disrupting a hydrogen bond with ubiquitin.
source: The mutation E10R reduces ubiquitination by TRIM25, possibly by disrupting a hydrogen bond with ubiquitin (Koliopoulos et al., 2016).
evidence: Supported by citation to Koliopoulos et al., 2016

claim: The E13R mutation reduces TRIM21 catalysis.
source: Consistent with this hypothesis, E13R reduced TRIM21 catalysis (Figure 2D).
evidence: Experimental data shown in Figure 2D

claim: The monomeric TRIM21 RING is a highly active E3.
source: Taken together these data show that the monomeric TRIM21 RING is a highly active E3.
evidence: Conclusion drawn from multiple experimental results

claim: The lack of constitutive TRIM21 NFκB activity is the result of tight regulation, independent of higher order oligomerisation.
source: Thus, the lack of constitutive TRIM21 NFκB activity must be the result of tight regulation, independent of higher order oligomerisation.
evidence: Conclusion inferred from the observation that monomeric RING is active but full-length protein is not

claim: The presence of the B-Box significantly reduces TRIM21 ubiquitination.
source: Comparing the activities of RING, RING-Box and MiniTRIM21 proteins (based on a monovalent MiniTRIM5 that preserves the Box-coiled coil interface (Wagner et al., 2016)), revealed that the presence of the B-Box significantly reduces ubiquitination (Figure 3A).
evidence: Experimental data shown in Figure 3A

claim: The B-Box prevents ubiquitin discharge from either Ube2D1 or Ube2N.
source: This is due to direct inhibition of catalytic activity, as the B-Box prevented ubiquitin discharge from either Ube2D1 or Ube2N (Figure 3B).
evidence: Experimental data shown in Figure 3B

claim: The crystal structure of TRIM21 RING-Box was solved at 2 Å resolution.
source: To understand how the B-Box modulates TRIM21 catalysis we solved a 2 Å crystal structure of the RING-Box protein (Supplementary file 1).
evidence: Experimental structural data

claim: The B-Box occupies the E2 binding site on the RING domain.
source: Surprisingly, this revealed that the B-Box occupies the E2 binding site on the RING domain (Figure 3C).
evidence: Structural data shown in Figure 3C

claim: The B-Box is located where helix 1 of the E2 would normally be positioned during RING binding.
source: Comparison to the TRIM5α RING:E2 complex shows that the B-Box is located where helix 1 of the E2 would normally be positioned during RING binding (Figure 3D).
evidence: Structural comparison shown in Figure 3D

claim: The B-Box acts as an E2 mimic by forming similar electrostatic interactions.
source: Crucially, the B-Box is able to occupy the E2 binding site on the RING by acting as an E2 mimic, forming similar electrostatic interactions.
evidence: Structural analysis and comparison

claim: Box-RING interaction is stabilized through a salt bridge between residues R118 and E12.
source: In particular, Box-RING interaction is stabilized through a salt bridge between residues R118 and E12, which is analogous to the interaction between E2 residue R14 and RING residue E11 in the TRIM5:Ube2N structure (Figure 3D).
evidence: Structural data shown in Figure 3D

claim: Titration of Ube2N into the RING resulted in significant chemical shift perturbations in E2 interface residues.
source: Titration of Ube2N into the RING resulted in significant CSPs in E2 interface residues (denoted by the green shaded regions in Figure 4A).
evidence: NMR experimental data shown in Figure 4A

claim: No evidence of Ube2N binding to the RING-Box was observed by NMR.
source: In contrast, no evidence of Ube2N binding to the RING-Box was observed.
evidence: NMR experimental data

claim: The B-Box is an autoinhibitory domain whose function is to regulate RING activity by preventing E2 recruitment.
source: Taken together, these data suggest that the B-Box may be an autoinhibitory domain whose function is to regulate RING activity by preventing E2 recruitment.
evidence: Conclusion inferred from structural and biochemical data

claim: MAVS, STING and TRIF all contain a short pLxIS motif that recruits kinases IKKβ or TBK1 resulting in serine phosphorylation and signal potentiation.
source: Recently it was shown that unrelated innate immune adaptors including MAVS, STING and TRIF all contain a short pLxIS motif (where p is hydrophilic, x is non-aromatic and S is the target serine), which recruits kinases IKKβ or TBK1 resulting in serine phosphorylation and signal potentiation (Liu et al., 2015).
evidence: Supported by citation to Liu et al., 2015

claim: TRIM21 contains a motif similar to the pLxIS motif at the end of its RING domain.
source: Remarkably, TRIM21 contains a very similar motif at the end of its RING domain.
evidence: Sequence analysis

claim: The target serine in the TRIM21 motif is located at the centre of the B-Box:RING interface.
source: Moreover, the target serine in this motif is located at the centre of the B-Box:RING interface (Figure 5A) and undergoes phosphorylation in cells (Figure 5B).
evidence: Structural data in Figure 5A and mass spectrometry data in Figure 5B

claim: TRIM21 serine 80 undergoes phosphorylation in cells.
source: Moreover, the target serine in this motif is located at the centre of the B-Box:RING interface (Figure 5A) and undergoes phosphorylation in cells (Figure 5B).
evidence: Mass spectrometry data shown in Figure 5B

claim: Cellular phosphorylation of TRIM21 but not S80A mutant was detected upon IKKβ overexpression.
source: Using this anti-pS80 serum, we detected cellular phosphorylation of TRIM21 but not an S80A mutant, upon IKKβ overexpression (Figure 5D).
evidence: Experimental data shown in Figure 5D

claim: Efficient IKKβ phosphorylation of TRIM21 was observed even under conditions where NFκB signaling was abolished.
source: Efficient IKKβ phosphorylation of TRIM21 was observed even under conditions where NFκB signaling was abolished (Figure 5E).
evidence: Experimental data shown in Figure 5E

claim: Recombinant IKKβ directly phosphorylates TRIM21 in vitro in an ATP-dependent manner.
source: To confirm that IKKβ directly phosphorylates TRIM21, we incubated recombinant RING-Box and IKKβ proteins in vitro, observing ATP-dependent IKKβ phosphorylation of TRIM21 that was lost upon mutation of motif residues or addition of an IKKβ inhibitor (Figure 5F–H).
evidence: In vitro kinase assay data shown in Figure 5F–H

claim: Robust IKKβ-mediated phosphorylation was observed using full-length TRIM21 protein.
source: Robust IKKβ-mediated phosphorylation was also observed using full-length TRIM21 protein (Figure 5I).
evidence: Experimental data shown in Figure 5I

claim: Knock-out of IKKβ by CRISPR/Cas9 abolished modification of overexpressed TRIM21-His.
source: Finally, knock-out of IKKβ by CRISPR/Cas9 abolished modification of overexpressed TRIM21-His (Figure 5J), suggesting that endogenous kinase phosphorylates TRIM21.
evidence: Experimental data shown in Figure 5J

claim: TBK1 is capable of phosphorylating TRIM21 in vitro comparably with IKKβ.
source: To test whether TRIM21 is a substrate for TBK1 phosphorylation, we incubated the recombinant full-length protein with the kinase in the presence of ATP. TBK1 was capable of phosphorylating TRIM21 in vitro comparably with IKKβ (Figure 6A).
evidence: In vitro kinase assay data shown in Figure 6A

claim: Overexpressed TBK1 was capable of strongly phosphorylating cellular TRIM21 and causing significant stabilization of the protein.
source: Overexpressed TBK1 was also capable of strongly phosphorylating cellular TRIM21 and causing significant stabilization of the protein (Figure 6B).
evidence: Experimental data shown in Figure 6B

claim: MAVS expression significantly increased phosphorylation of TRIM21.
source: First, we stimulated the TBK1 pathway by expressing one of its upstream adaptors, MAVS. MAVS expression significantly increased phosphorylation of TRIM21 (Figure 6C).
evidence: Experimental data shown in Figure 6C

claim: A rapid increase in TRIM21 phosphorylation was observed upon poly(I:C) stimulation.
source: Second, we stimulated cells with the MDA5/RIG-I ligand poly(I:C) (Kato et al., 2008). We observed a rapid increase in TRIM21 phosphorylation upon poly(I:C) stimulation, consistent with TBK1 activation (Figure 6D).
evidence: Experimental data shown in Figure 6D

claim: There is a significant increase in the proportion of phosphorylated TRIM21 following infection with antibody-coated adenovirus.
source: Finally, we monitored changes in TRIM21 phosphorylation following infection with antibody-coated adenovirus, under conditions where we have previously demonstrated TRIM21-dependent antiviral activity (McEwan et al., 2013). The data show that in equivalent levels of immunoprecipitated TRIM21 there is a significant increase in the proportion of phosphorylated TRIM21 (Figure 6E).
evidence: Experimental data shown in Figure 6E

claim: Introduction of S80E into the RING-Box was sufficient to completely restore catalytic activity to the same level as the RING alone.
source: Remarkably, introduction of S80E into the RING-Box was sufficient to completely restore catalytic activity to the same level as the RING alone (Figure 7A–B).
evidence: Experimental data shown in Figure 7A–B

claim: S80 phosphorylation potentiates TRIM21 ubiquitination activity.
source: Comparison with wild-type protein revealed that S80 phosphorylation potentiates TRIM21 ubiquitination activity (Figure 7C).
evidence: Experimental data using co-translationally incorporated phosphoserine shown in Figure 7C

claim: Treating phosphorylated TRIM21 with phosphatase dephosphorylated S80 and restored autoinhibition.
source: Phosphorylation-dependence was confirmed by treating the phosphoprotein with phosphatase, which dephosphorylated S80 and restored autoinhibition (Figure 7C).
evidence: Experimental data shown in Figure 7C

claim: Modification of S80 is sufficient to control ubiquitination activity of TRIM21 in the presence of the B-Box.
source: Taken together, this show that modification of S80 is sufficient to control ubiquitination activity of TRIM21 in the presence of the B-Box.
evidence: Conclusion drawn from phosphorylation and phosphomimetic experiments

claim: Mutant S80E can be used as a functional mimic of serine phosphorylation at position 80.
source: Moreover, mutant S80E can be used as a functional mimic of serine phosphorylation at position 80.
evidence: Conclusion drawn from comparison of S80E and phosphoserine data

claim: Neither S80A nor wild-type TRIM21 triggered NFκB, but S80E conferred robust activation.
source: Neither S80A nor wild-type TRIM21 triggered NFκB, but S80E conferred robust activation (Figure 8A).
evidence: Experimental data shown in Figure 8A

claim: Mutation of residue S80 did not alter virus neutralization.
source: In contrast, mutation of residue S80 did not alter virus neutralization (Figure 8B).
evidence: Experimental data shown in Figure 8B

claim: Significant TNFA induction was only observed during infection in the presence of antibody, and not in TRIM21 knockout cells.
source: Significant TNFA induction was only observed during infection in the presence of antibody, and not in TRIM21 knockout cells (K21, Figure 8C and Figure 8—figure supplement 1).
evidence: Experimental data shown in Figure 8C and Figure 8—figure supplement 1

claim: Expression of S80A failed to rescue TNFA induction, while S80E enabled TNFA induction beyond wild-type levels.
source: Importantly, expression of S80A failed to rescue TNFA induction, while S80E enabled TNFA induction beyond wild-type levels.
evidence: Experimental data from infection experiments

claim: Expression of wild-type TRIM21 in knockout cells increased TNFA induction upon infection with HRV + antibody.
source: As with AdV, expression of wild-type TRIM21 in knockout cells increased TNFA induction upon infection with HRV + antibody (Figure 8D).
evidence: Experimental data shown in Figure 8D

claim: Mutant S80E greatly potentiated TNFA transcription while S80A failed to reconstitute TRIM21 activity during HRV infection.
source: Mutant S80E greatly potentiated TNFA transcription while S80A failed to reconstitute TRIM21 activity.
evidence: Experimental data from HRV infection experiments

claim: Similar results to TNFA were obtained for cytokines CXCL10 and IL6 and the interferon-stimulated gene IFIT1 during HRV infection.
source: Similar results were obtained for cytokines CXCL10 and IL6 and the interferon-stimulated gene IFIT1.
evidence: Experimental data from HRV infection experiments

claim: Significant chemical shift perturbations were detected in canonical E2 binding site residues upon titration of Ube2N into S80E RING-Box.
source: In contrast to wild-type, we detected significant CSPs in canonical E2 binding site residues upon titration of Ube2N into S80E (Figure 9A).
evidence: NMR experimental data shown in Figure 9A

claim: There were changes in residues at the base of helix 2, within the linker and on B-Box residues that contact the RING in S80E upon E2 binding.
source: There were also changes in residues at the base of helix 2, within the linker and on B-Box residues that contact the RING.
evidence: NMR experimental data

claim: The most dynamic region in TRIM21 RING-Box is the linker (residues 83–102) between the RING and B-Box.
source: The {1H}15N NOE ratios reveal that the most dynamic region is the linker (residues 83–102) between the RING and B-Box (Figure 9B).
evidence: NMR relaxation data shown in Figure 9B

claim: Mutant S80E has markedly lower enhancement factors both in the linker region and in helix 1.
source: Importantly, mutant S80E has markedly lower enhancement factors both in the linker region and in helix 1 (residues 1–17), against which the B-Box packs (Figure 9B).
evidence: NMR relaxation data shown in Figure 9B

claim: The S80E mutation caused a dramatic change in surface accessibility precisely localized to the RING-Box interface.
source: The S80E mutation caused a dramatic change in surface accessibility precisely localized to the RING-Box interface (Figure 9C and Supplementary file 2).
evidence: Paramagnetic relaxation enhancement experimental data shown in Figure 9C

claim: Phosphomimetic mutation at serine 80 disrupts the RING:Box interaction and uncovers the E2 binding site.
source: These data confirm that phosphomimetic mutation at serine 80 disrupts the RING:Box interaction and uncovers the E2 binding site.
evidence: Conclusion drawn from multiple NMR experiments

claim: Intracellular antibody immune signalling is kept in check via tight regulation of the cytosolic antibody receptor TRIM21.
source: Our results suggest intracellular antibody immune signalling is kept in check via tight regulation of the cytosolic antibody receptor TRIM21.
evidence: Summary conclusion from all experimental results

claim: TRIM21 is kept in a constitutively silent state through an autoinhibitory mechanism that blocks E2 enzyme recruitment.
source: Here we have shown that this is accomplished by keeping TRIM21 in a constitutively silent state through an autoinhibitory mechanism that blocks E2 enzyme recruitment.
evidence: Summary conclusion from experimental results

claim: Autoinhibition is mediated by the B-Box, providing a function for this ubiquitous but hitherto enigmatic TRIM protein domain.
source: Autoinhibition is mediated by the B-Box, providing a function for this ubiquitous but hitherto enigmatic TRIM protein domain.
evidence: Summary conclusion from structural and biochemical data

claim: The B-Box inhibits E2 recruitment by acting as an E2 mimic and competing for RING binding.
source: The B-Box inhibits E2 recruitment by acting as an E2 mimic and competing for RING binding.
evidence: Conclusion from structural and biochemical data

claim: Phosphorylation of S80 or its replacement by a phosphomimetic displaces the B-Box, allowing E2 recruitment.
source: Phosphorylation of S80 or its replacement by a phosphomimetic displaces the B-Box, allowing E2 recruitment and potentiating TRIM21 ubiquitination activity, NF-κB signalling and cytokine transcription upon infection with DNA or RNA viruses.
evidence: Summary conclusion from multiple experimental approaches

claim: TRIM21 may undergo clustering via cross-linking or higher order assembly when recruited to opsonized pathogens.
source: TRIM21 may also undergo clustering, via cross-linking or higher order assembly, when it is recruited to opsonized pathogens.
evidence: Speculation about mechanism

claim: TRIM21 could participate in its own positive-feedback loop through co-option of IKKβ and TBK1 as amplifying kinases.
source: The co-option of IKKβ and TBK1 as amplifying kinases suggests that TRIM21 could participate in its own positive-feedback loop.
evidence: Speculation based on kinase identity

claim: TRIM21 has been shown to synergise with cytosolic nucleic acid receptors such as RIG-I and cGAS.
source: Similarly, TRIM21 has been shown to synergise with cytosolic nucleic acid receptors such as RIG-I and cGAS, resulting in pathogen-specific responses and multiple signalling waves (Watkinson et al., 2015).
evidence: Supported by citation to Watkinson et al., 2015

claim: TRIM RINGs, including those of TRIM5, 25 and 32, are active in vitro at concentrations where they are monomeric.
source: TRIM RINGs, including those of TRIM5, 25 and 32, are active in vitro at concentrations where they are monomeric (Yudina et al., 2015; Sanchez et al., 2016; Koliopoulos et al., 2016).
evidence: Supported by citations to multiple studies

claim: TRIM21 signalling has a distinct threshold whereas neutralization takes place at very low antibody occupancy.
source: Previously we have observed that TRIM21 signalling has a distinct threshold whereas neutralization takes place at very low antibody occupancy (<2 antibodies) (McEwan et al., 2012) and under conditions of sub-optimal TRIM21:antibody and antibody:antigen kinetics (Foss et al., 2016; Bottermann et al., 2016).
evidence: Supported by citations to previous work

claim: Basal activity via higher order assembly may be sufficient for neutralization but not signalling.
source: Therefore, basal activity via higher order assembly may be sufficient for neutralization but not signalling.
evidence: Speculation based on differential thresholds

claim: TRIM21 is activated by leaked immune complexes in lysosome-maturation-defective macrophages of lupus-prone mice.
source: The activation of TRIM21 by leaked immune complexes in lysosome-maturation-defective macrophages of lupus-prone mice illustrates the consequences of such an event (Monteith et al., 2016).
evidence: Supported by citation to Monteith et al., 2016
